title: High Parallel Complexity Graphs and Memory-Hard Functions
authors: Joël Alwen, Vladimir Serbinenko

findings.claim: Cumulative pebbling complexity (memory summed over time) captures parallel cost where older pebbling measures fail.
findings.quote: cumulative complexity (CC) and show how it overcomes a crucial shortcoming in the parallel setting exhibited by more traditional complexity measures used in past reductions.
findings.bears_on: Depth-robust-graph arguments from memory-hard functions are a route to NCI-style bounds for computations whose dependency DAG is depth-robust, as sequential SGD's may be.

title: Minimizing Communication in Linear Algebra
authors: Grey Ballard, James Demmel, Olga Holtz, Oded Schwartz

findings.claim: For a large class of direct linear algebra, communication is at least the arithmetic count divided by the square root of the fast (or local) memory size.
findings.quote: In both cases the lower bound may be expressed as $\Omega$(#arithmetic operations / $\sqrt{M}$), where $M$ is the size of the fast memory (or local memory in the parallel case).

quantities.condition: communication >= (#arithmetic operations) / M^0.5; Loomis-Whitney segment argument

findings.bears_on: The segment argument (bound work per segment of M loads, divide total work by it) is exactly how an NCI slowdown bound is built: bound useful training progress per block given K novel bits, then count blocks.

findings.claim: Within a segment, the number of multiply-adds is bounded by the geometric mean of the three operand projections (Loomis-Whitney).
findings.quote: Let $|\cdot|$ denote the cardinality of a set. Then $|V|\leq\sqrt{|A_{x}|\cdot|A_{y}|\cdot|A_{z}|}$.
findings.bears_on: With committed weights free, one projection is unbounded and NCI does not cap outputs, so this inequality degenerates to a bound linear in the novel input; NCI's bounds must come from dependency structure instead.

findings.claim: Operands created and discarded inside a segment cannot be bounded by the segment argument without extra structure.
findings.quote: The S2/D2 operands, those created during the segment and then discarded without causing any slow memory traffic, cannot be bounded without further information.
findings.bears_on: Matches NCI's setting in which intermediates inside a Gamma-gate block are free; NCI bounds cannot rely on charging for in-block intermediates.

title: Graph Expansion and Communication Costs of Fast Matrix Multiplication
authors: Grey Ballard, James Demmel, Olga Holtz, Oded Schwartz
venue: Journal of the ACM 59(6) (SPAA 2011 best paper; arXiv 1109.1693)

findings.claim: Communication cost is governed by the edge expansion of the computation graph.
findings.quote: The communication cost of algorithms (also known as I/O-complexity) is shown to be closely related to the expansion properties of the corresponding computation graphs.
findings.bears_on: Expansion of the training circuit's DAG (how many edges leave any small set of gates) is a candidate route to NCI bounds that survive restructuring of matrix products.

findings.claim: Strassen-like algorithms need Omega((n/sqrt(M))^omega0 * M) communication, p times less with p processors.
findings.quote: where $\omega_{0}$ is the exponent in the arithmetic count (e.g., $\omega_{0}=\lg 7$ for Strassen, and $\omega_{0}=3$ for conventional matrix multiplication). With $p$ parallel processors, each with fast memory of size $M$, the lower bound is $p$ times smaller.

quantities.condition: derived: lg 7 = 2.807 for Strassen; omega0 = 3 for conventional

findings.bears_on: Shows how to extend a per-piece bound to fast bilinear algorithms; an NCI bound on matrix-product-heavy training should hold for any bilinear restructuring an adversary might choose.

findings.claim: The expansion approach forbids recomputation, a serious gap for NCI where a block has Gamma gates to recompute freely.
findings.quote: We were not able to allow recomputation using our edge expansion approach.
findings.bears_on: Expansion bounds cannot be imported into NCI as is; NCI must allow recomputation, which pushes toward the Grigoriev-flow (Bilardi-De Stefani) or communication-complexity (Saha-Ye) techniques.

findings.claim: Loomis-Whitney counting fails once an algorithm uses distributivity, as Strassen's does.
findings.quote: approach, however, is not suitable when distributivity is used, as is the case in Strassen
findings.bears_on: Geometric counting of products is not robust to algebraic restructuring; NCI proofs should not depend on the circuit computing matrix products the classical way.

title: Communication Steps for Parallel Query Processing
authors: Paul Beame, Paraschos Koutris, Dan Suciu

findings.claim: In the MPC model each server receives O(n/p^(1-epsilon)) bits per round, epsilon controlling replication; one-round evaluation of a query q needs epsilon >= 1 - 1/tau*.
findings.quote: we show that any algorithm requires ε ≥ 1--1/τ*, where τ* is the fractional vertex cover of the hypergraph of q
findings.bears_on: Replication-based lower bounds charge for copying input data; NCI does not charge for committed data, so the analogous NCI bound must charge only computed data that crosses blocks.

findings.claim: With near-linear per-processor load, Omega(log p) rounds are needed for some queries.
findings.quote: per-processor load that is O (m/p 1-ε ) requires Ω(log p) rounds of communication.
findings.bears_on: Round-versus-load tradeoffs correspond to NCI's depth-versus-K tradeoff: a smaller K forces a longer chain of dependent blocks.

title: xLSTM Scaling Laws: Competitive Performance with Linear Time-Complexity
authors: Maximilian Beck, Kajetan Schweighofer, Sebastian Böck, Sebastian Lehner, Sepp Hochreiter

findings.claim: Across 80M-7B parameters and 2B-2T tokens, xLSTM Pareto-dominates Transformers in loss per compute.
findings.quote: Notably, xLSTM models consistently Pareto-dominate Transformer models, delivering lower cross-entropy loss for the same compute budget.
findings.bears_on: Recurrent m_A slightly above 1; the authors' own comparison.

title: Logical Depth and Physical Complexity
authors: Charles H. Bennett
venue: The Universal Turing Machine: A Half-Century Survey (ed. R. Herken), Oxford University Press

findings.claim: Logical depth is the time a universal machine needs to produce an object from an algorithmically random input.
findings.quote: defining an object’s “logical depth” as the time required by a standard universal Turing machine to gen erate it from an input that is algorithmically random
findings.bears_on: Trained weights are deep objects in Bennett's sense; NCI targets the accumulation of depth (training) while letting shallow, prompt-driven computation (inference) through.

findings.claim: Depth obeys a slow-growth law: deep objects cannot be produced quickly from shallow ones.
findings.quote: slow-growth law: deep objects cannot be quickly produced from shallow ones by any deterministic process, nor with much probability by a probabilistic process, but can be pro duced slowly.
findings.bears_on: Suggests a per-block invariant (depth gained relative to theta is at most the block's work) that NCI could aim for; depth is uncomputable, so NCI's cap on novel input is the enforceable proxy.

title: Chinchilla Scaling: A replication attempt
authors: Tamay Besiroglu, Ege Erdil, Matthew Barnett, Josh You

findings.claim: Chinchilla's Approach 3 fit is inconsistent with its other two methods; a refit agrees with them.
findings.quote: We find that the reported estimates are inconsistent with their first two estimation methods, fail at fitting the extracted data, and report implausibly narrow confidence intervals
findings.bears_on: The reference allocation is robust (Approaches 1-2), though fitted constants carry wide uncertainty.

title: The I/O complexity of Strassen's matrix multiplication with recomputation
authors: Gianfranco Bilardi, Lorenzo De Stefani

findings.claim: The Strassen I/O bound holds even when recomputation is allowed, proved via the Grigoriev flow of the matrix multiplication function rather than graph expansion.
findings.quote: The result generalizes a similar bound previously obtained under the constraint of no-recomputation, that is, that intermediate results cannot be computed more than once.
findings.bears_on: The Grigoriev-flow technique is a property of the function, not of one circuit, so it is the right shape for NCI, where blocks may recompute anything within Gamma gates.

title: Communication Lower Bounds for Statistical Estimation Problems via a Distributed Data Processing Inequality
authors: Mark Braverman, Ankit Garg, Tengyu Ma, Huy L. Nguyen, David P. Woodruff

findings.claim: Distributed sparse linear regression over m machines with n observations each needs total communication Omega(min{n,d} m) to reach minimax error, proved with a distributed strong data processing inequality.
findings.quote: to achieve the statistical minimax error, the total communication is at least $\Omega(\min\{n,d\}m)$, where $n$ is the number of observations that each machine
findings.bears_on: Strong data processing inequalities bound information rather than words, the quantity NCI caps; they could give lower bounds on the novel bits per block for learning tasks independent of the compression scheme.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim yes, quantities n/a

title: Distillation Scaling Laws
authors: Dan Busbridge, Amitis Shidani, Floris Weers, Jason Ramapuram, Etai Littwin, Russ Webb

findings.claim: With an existing teacher, distillation beats supervised training up to a compute level that grows with student size; if the teacher must also be trained, supervised training is generally better.
findings.quote: In settings involving many students or an existing teacher, distillation outperforms supervised learning up to a compute level that scales predictably with student size. Conversely, if only one student is to be distilled and a teacher also requires training, supervised learning is generally preferable.
findings.bears_on: Distillation's m_A exceeds 1 only below a crossover compute and only when the teacher is sunk cost.

findings.claim: Given enough student compute or tokens, supervised training beats distillation; distillation wins only on modest token budgets.
findings.quote: Supervised learning always outperforms distillation given enough student compute or tokens. For a modest token budget, distillation is favorable; however, when a large number of tokens are available, supervised learning outperforms distillation.
findings.bears_on: A free registered teacher raises a student's compute multiplier only below a crossover; at frontier-scale budgets the student is better off training on data.

findings.claim: Weak-to-strong gains appear only with finite distillation data; with enough tokens the student's loss rises back to the teacher's.
findings.quote: weak-to-strong generalization (Burns et al., 2024; Ildiz et al., 2024) occurs only in the finite distillation data regime, and when the number of tokens is sufficiently large, the student cross-entropy increases again, eventually matching the teacher cross-entropy.
findings.bears_on: Distillation from a registered teacher does not carry a student below the teacher's loss at scale.

findings.claim: The fitted distillation law's teacher-dependence constants (with 95% intervals), fitted on 73 supervised and 697 distillation runs on C4.
findings.bears_on: Constants for solving the law for the student compute that reaches a target loss above the teacher's; the law keeps L_S > L_T, so targets at or below the teacher are unreachable.

findings.claim: When teacher training is discounted, distillation often costs less: about 3/4 the compute of supervised training for a 500M student at cross-entropy 2.4 and about 1/2 for a 10B student at 2.2.
findings.quote: When teacher training is discounted, distillation is often more efficient.

quantities.unit: compute multiplier, student-side (supervised over distillation compute)
quantities.condition: 10B student at cross-entropy 2.2, teacher discounted (Figure 33)

findings.bears_on: Student-side multipliers of about 1.3-2 when the teacher is free, for targets above the teacher's loss. The paper's scenario labels around Figure 33 conflict, so the 3/4 and 1/2 figures are uncertain.

findings.claim: Capacity gap: a better teacher does not always make a better student, and can make it worse.
findings.quote: we observe the capacity gap, where improving teacher performance does not always improve student performance, and even reduces student performance eventually.
findings.bears_on: The strongest registered model is not automatically the best teacher; reuse gains saturate.

findings.claim: The compute at which supervised learning overtakes distillation grows with student size.
findings.quote: The compute transition point at which supervised learning becomes preferable to distillation increases as a function of student size.
findings.bears_on: Larger students keep distillation's advantage longer, so the frontier-scale crossover is an extrapolation.

title: Communication lower bounds and optimal algorithms for programs that reference arrays -- Part 1
authors: Michael Christ, James Demmel, Nicholas Knight, Thomas Scanlon, Katherine Yelick

findings.claim: Discrete Holder-Brascamp-Lieb inequalities generalize Loomis-Whitney and give communication lower bounds for any loop nest whose array indices are affine in the loop variables.
findings.quote: Using a recent generalization of Loomis’ and Whitney’s result, we generalize this lower bound approach to a much larger class of algorithms, that may have arbitrary numbers of loops and arrays with arbitrary dimensions, as long as the index expressions are affine combinations of loop variables.
findings.bears_on: HBL inequalities with weights let one projection be free and still bound the others, a possible way to bound attention and convolution work per NCI block when only the activation projections are capped.

title: Unified Scaling Laws for Routed Language Models
authors: Aidan Clark, Diego de las Casas, Aurelia Guy, Arthur Mensch, Michela Paganini, Jordan Hoffmann et al.

findings.claim: All three routing techniques predict diminishing improvement from routing as base model size grows.
findings.quote: All three routing techniques considered therefore predict diminishing improvements from routing when increasing scale.
findings.bears_on: Older routing (fixed 130B tokens, coarse experts) gives MoE m_A that shrinks with scale.

findings.claim: Routing stops helping beyond a cutoff size of 937B (S-BASE), 85B (RL-R) and 83B (HASH) parameters at 130B tokens.
findings.quote: Ncutoff equals 937B, 85B and 83B for S - BASE, RL - R and HASH respectively. These values are highly dependent on the number of tokens seen

quantities.condition: routing cutoff, S-BASE, 130B tokens

findings.bears_on: The counterpoint to Krajewski: MoE m_A could vanish at large N under fixed-token training.

title: DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
authors: Damai Dai, Chengqi Deng, Chenggang Zhao, R. X. Xu, Huazuo Gao, Deli Chen et al.

findings.claim: DeepSeekMoE 16B matches LLaMA2 7B with about 40% of the computation.
findings.quote: Subsequently, we scale up DeepSeekMoE to 16B parameters and show that it achieves comparable performance with LLaMA2 7B, with only about 40% of computations.

quantities.condition: derived 1/0.40: DeepSeekMoE 16B vs LLaMA2 7B

findings.bears_on: Fine-grained plus shared experts: m_A about 2.5 against a dense model on different data.

title: Transformers are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms Through Structured State Space Duality
authors: Tri Dao, Albert Gu

findings.claim: Mamba-2's SSD layer is 2-8x faster than Mamba's selective SSM and stays competitive with Transformers.
findings.quote: a new architecture (Mamba-2) whose core layer is an a refinement of Mamba's selective SSM that is 2-8X faster, while continuing to be competitive with Transformers on language modeling
findings.bears_on: Throughput gain, not a per-FLOP m_A; loss per FLOP is about the reference.

title: Distributed Verification and Hardness of Distributed Approximation
authors: Atish Das Sarma, Stephan Holzer, Liah Kor, Amos Korman, Danupon Nanongkai, Gopal Pandurangan, et al.

findings.claim: In CONGEST with B-bit messages, many verification problems need Omega(sqrt(n/(B log n)) + D) rounds, proved by reduction from two-party communication complexity across a bottleneck.
findings.quote: We show a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{n/(B\log n)}+D)$ for many verification problems in the $B$ model
findings.bears_on: The reduction from set disjointness across a cut is a technique for lower-bounding the novel bits that must cross any NCI block boundary for a given update function.

findings.claim: In distributed settings verification can be harder than computation.
findings.quote: verification is harder than computation in the distributed world!
findings.bears_on: Cautions that per-block checks need not be cheap in a distributed setting; NCI places verification outside the bandwidth-limited model, with committed state and a proof service.

title: AI capabilities can be significantly improved without expensive retraining
authors: Tom Davidson, Jean-Stanislas Denain, Pablo Villalobos, Guillem Bas

findings.claim: Defines compute-equivalent gain as the extra training compute that would match an enhancement's benefit.
findings.quote: the compute-equivalent gain: how much additional training compute would be needed to improve performance by the same amount as the enhancement
findings.bears_on: The unit of m_A used throughout this corpus.

title: Griffin: Mixing Gated Linear Recurrences with Local Attention for Efficient Language Models
authors: Soham De, Samuel L. Smith, Anushan Fernando, Aleksandar Botev, George Cristian-Muraru, Albert Gu et al.

findings.claim: Griffin (gated linear recurrence plus local attention) has the lowest held-out loss at every FLOP budget against an MQA Transformer baseline, up to 14B parameters.
findings.quote: Hawk, Griffin and our MQA Transformer baseline all show power law scaling between held-out loss and training FLOPs, with Griffin achieving the lowest held-out loss at all FLOPs budgets.
findings.bears_on: Hybrid recurrent m_A slightly above 1 and constant across about 1e18-1e21 FLOP.

title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
authors: William Fedus, Barret Zoph, Noam Shazeer

findings.claim: Switch Transformers based on T5-Base and T5-Large get up to 7x pre-training speedups at equal compute.
findings.quote: We design models based off T5-Base and T5-Large to obtain up to 7x increases in pre-training speed with the same computational resources.

quantities.condition: Switch vs T5-Base, step-time speedup to equal quality

findings.bears_on: Top-1 MoE m_A up to 7 at T5-Base scale.

title: Extractor-Based Time-Space Lower Bounds for Learning
authors: Sumegha Garg, Ran Raz, Avishay Tal

findings.claim: For any learning problem whose sample-concept matrix is a (k, l)-extractor with error 2^-r, a learner needs either Omega(k l) memory or 2^Omega(r) samples.
findings.quote: We show that any learning algorithm for the learning problem corresponding to $M$ requires either a memory of size at least $\Omega\left(k\cdot\ell\right)$, or at least $2^{\Omega(r)}$ samples.
findings.bears_on: Generalizes Raz's bound to a broad class of learning problems, so a K-bit cross-block state is a hard bottleneck for any task with extractor structure, not only parities.
findings.audit: 2026-10-17 sample audit: quote yes, claim yes, quantities n/a

findings.claim: The bound is tight at memory about (log|X|)(log|A|) for many problems.
findings.quote: achieving a tight $\Omega\left((\log|X|)\cdot(\log|A|)\right)$ lower bound on the size of the memory
findings.bears_on: Suggests the memory threshold scales like (bits per sample) x (bits per concept), which for LLM training would be (b_tok x context) x (bits of model), far above K; whether real LLM training has extractor structure is open.

title: Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach
authors: Jonas Geiping, Sean McLeish, Neel Jain, John Kirchenbauer, Siddharth Singh, Brian R. Bartoldson et al.

findings.claim: A 3.5B recurrent-depth model trained on 800B tokens can use test-time iterations up to a compute load equivalent to 50B parameters.
findings.quote: We scale a proof-of-concept model to 3.5 billion parameters and 800 billion tokens. We show that the resulting model can improve its performance on reasoning benchmarks, sometimes dramatically, up to a computation load equivalent to 50 billion parameters.
findings.bears_on: Looping raises FLOPs per updated parameter; few updated weights carry many gates of work.

title: Better & Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction
authors: Fabian Gloeckle, Badr Youbi Idrissi, Baptiste Rozière, David Lopez-Paz, Gabriel Synnaeve

findings.claim: Multi-token prediction becomes more useful with model size.
findings.quote: The method is increasingly useful for larger model sizes, and keeps its appeal when training for multiple epochs.
findings.bears_on: An objective whose benefit grows with N, though on generative benchmarks.

findings.claim: 13B models trained with multi-token prediction solve 12% more HumanEval and 17% more MBPP problems.
findings.quote: Our 13B parameter models solves 12 % more problems on HumanEval and 17 % more on MBPP than comparable next-token models.
findings.bears_on: Task gain, not a loss-based compute ratio.

title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
authors: Albert Gu, Tri Dao

findings.claim: Under the Chinchilla protocol from about 125M to 1.3B parameters, Mamba matches a Transformer++ recipe.
findings.quote: Mamba is the first attention-free model to match the performance of a very strong Transformer recipe (Transformer++) that has now become standard, particularly as the sequence length grows.
findings.bears_on: Selective SSMs give m_A about 1 at small scale; their per-token state is a fixed-size recurrent state.

findings.claim: Mamba-3B outperforms same-size Transformers and matches Transformers twice its size.
findings.quote: On language modeling, our Mamba-3B model outperforms Transformers of the same size and matches Transformers twice its size, both in pretraining and downstream evaluation.
findings.bears_on: Against a Pythia-style baseline at fixed tokens; not a compute-optimal comparison.

title: On the Origin of Algorithmic Progress in AI
authors: Hans Gundlach, Alex Fogelson, Jayson Lynch, Ana Trisovic, Jonathan Rosenfeld, Anmol Sandhu et al.

findings.claim: Small-scale ablations account for under 10x of the estimated 22,000x algorithmic gain; most of the gain is scale-dependent, dominated by the LSTM-to-Transformer transition.
findings.quote: Running small-scale ablation experiments on key innovations from this time period, we are able to account for less than 10× of these gains.

quantities.condition: upper bound on the product of ablated scale-invariant gains at 3.6M parameters

findings.bears_on: Most catalogued innovations give small constant m_A; only a few scale-dependent ones matter at frontier C.

findings.claim: SwiGLU gives a 1.17x compute-equivalent gain over GeLU in a 3.6M-parameter transformer.
findings.quote: we find that SwiGLU, has a measurable 1.17× efficiency gain over GeLU even taking into account its increased parameter requirements

quantities.condition: SwiGLU vs GeLU at 3.6M parameters, loss threshold 5.3

findings.bears_on: Small constant m_A for an architecture tweak; no change to NCI state.

findings.claim: Rotary position encoding gives about 1.44x over sinusoidal encoding.
findings.quote: We estimate that rotary encoding constitutes an improvement of 44% in training efficiency over sinusoidal encoding originally employed in Vaswani et al. [2017].

quantities.condition: RoPE vs sinusoidal at 3.6M parameters

findings.bears_on: Small constant m_A; no change to NCI state.

findings.claim: Learning-rate schedule choice changes training efficiency by under 5%.
findings.quote: We observe very small training efficiency gains between any learning rate schedules (< 5%).

quantities.condition: upper bound across inverse-sqrt, linear and cosine schedules

findings.bears_on: Schedules give m_A near 1.

findings.claim: Pre-RMSNorm gives 1.87x over post-RMSNorm, and 1.09x over pre-LayerNorm.
findings.quote: We observe substantial improvements of 87% transitioning from post-RMSNorm to pre-RMSNorm, with more modest improvements of 9% switching from a pre-layernorm model to a pre-RMSNorm model.

quantities.condition: pre-RMSNorm vs post-RMSNorm
pre-RMSNorm vs pre-LayerNorm

findings.bears_on: Moderate constant m_A from normalization placement.

findings.claim: AdamW is 1.87x more compute-efficient than well-tuned momentum SGD, and the gap is roughly scale-invariant.
findings.quote: we observe smoother scaling behavior and a sizable 1.87× gap in training efficiency compared to AdamW

quantities.condition: AdamW vs SGD (momentum 0.98, batch 64) at 3.6M parameters

findings.bears_on: Adaptive optimizer state (2 extra fp32 words per parameter) buys about 1.9x; dropping it (SGD) lowers state_bits_per_param at that cost.

findings.claim: Gains do not multiply: reverting four post-2017 changes predicts 3.43x but measures 1.33x.
findings.quote: Using the estimates in Figure 1 and assuming multiplicative improvement we would expect CEG gains of 3.43×. However, the efficiency gain is only 1.33×.

quantities.condition: Modern vs Retro transformer measured; 3.43x predicted by multiplying ablations

findings.bears_on: Composite m_A for stacked tweaks is sub-multiplicative; summing log-multipliers overstates C_eff.

findings.claim: MoE's FLOP-efficiency gain is estimated at or below 2x at a fixed number of experts.
findings.quote: However, we estimate that this is at or below a 2× factor in FLOP efficiency holding the number of experts constant.

quantities.condition: MoE vs dense, literature estimate, fixed expert count

findings.bears_on: Conservative m_A for MoE, against Krajewski's larger scale-dependent figures.

findings.claim: The LSTM-to-Transformer gap grows from 6.28x at the smallest scale to 26x at a lower loss threshold.
findings.quote: Interestingly, our LSTM model at the smallest scales we measure is only 6.28× less compute-efficient than our transformer model (using a loss threshold of 5.3 or above, see Section 3.1). While at a validation threshold of 4.4, the efficiency gap is 26×

quantities.condition: Modern transformer vs LSTM, loss threshold 5.3
Modern transformer vs LSTM, loss threshold 4.4

findings.bears_on: A scale-dependent (exponent-change) multiplier: m_A grows with C, so it matters most to a well-resourced adversary.

findings.claim: Moving from Kaplan to Chinchilla allocation is scale-dependent but stays under 10x over 1e16-1e24 FLOP.
findings.quote: Furthermore, the Chinchilla training efficiency gains are large but remain below 10x for much of the scale used in contemporary machine learning (i.e., 10^16 − 10^24 FLOPs).

quantities.condition: upper bound of Chinchilla vs Kaplan allocation gain, 1e16-1e24 FLOP

findings.bears_on: Compute allocation is a data/size choice with no NCI cost of its own; its m_A grows with C.

findings.claim: Adam vs SGD and modern vs retro transformer gains are roughly scale-invariant.
findings.quote: Meanwhile, the choice between Adam and SGD, as well as the difference between a modern and a Retro Transformer, seems to be relatively scale-invariant.
findings.bears_on: Optimizer and tweak multipliers are constant in C.

title: Scaling Laws and Compute-Optimal Training Beyond Fixed Training Durations
authors: Alexander Hägele, Elie Bakouch, Atli Kosson, Loubna Ben Allal, Leandro Von Werra, Martin Jaggi

findings.claim: A constant learning rate with a cooldown scales predictably and like cosine.
findings.quote: We investigate the training behavior of a direct alternative -- constant learning rate and cooldowns -- and find that it scales predictably and reliably similar to cosine.
findings.bears_on: Schedules give m_A about 1; their gain is reusable runs for fitting laws.

title: Measuring the Algorithmic Efficiency of Neural Networks
authors: Danny Hernandez, Tom B. Brown

findings.claim: Compute to reach AlexNet-level ImageNet accuracy fell 44x from 2012 to 2019.
findings.quote: the number of floating-point operations required to train a classifier to AlexNet-level performance on ImageNet has decreased by a factor of 44x between 2012 and 2019

quantities.condition: ImageNet AlexNet-level compute reduction 2012-2019

findings.bears_on: Measures m_A at a fixed old capability, which favours scale-invariant innovations.

title: Algorithmic progress in language models
authors: Anson Ho, Tamay Besiroglu, Ege Erdil, David Owen, Robi Rahman, Zifan Carl Guo et al.

findings.claim: Across 200+ evaluations on WikiText and Penn Treebank (2012-2023), the compute to reach a fixed perplexity halved about every 8 months.
findings.quote: we find that the compute required to reach a set performance threshold has halved approximately every 8 months, with a 95% confidence interval of around 5 to 14 months

quantities.condition: halving time of compute to fixed perplexity; 95% CI 5-14 months

findings.bears_on: Sets the background rate of m_A growth an adversary could ride under a fixed compute cap; the estimate pools all innovations and does not say which ones survive at frontier scale.

findings.claim: The transformer's compute-equivalent gain over earlier architectures is about 7x (CI 3-46x) at frontier budgets, and 6.6x at lower budgets.
findings.quote: Based on 100 bootstraps, we obtain a median estimate of 7.2× [95% CI: 3.3×, 45.7×] for the transformer’s compute-equivalent gain.

quantities.condition: transformer vs LSTM/RNN/SSM compute-equivalent gain, 95% CI 3.3-45.7

findings.bears_on: The largest single architecture multiplier in the record; m_A for the reference recipe already includes it.

title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
authors: Jordan Hoffmann, Sebastian Borgeaud, Arthur Mensch, Elena Buchatskaya, Trevor Cai, Eliza Rutherford et al.

findings.claim: Compute-optimal training scales parameters and tokens equally.
findings.quote: we find that for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled

quantities.condition: N_opt ∝ C^0.5, D_opt ∝ C^0.5

findings.bears_on: Defines the reference allocation (about 20 tokens per parameter).

title: I/O complexity: The red-blue pebble game
authors: Jia-Wei Hong, H. T. Kung

findings.claim: The red-blue pebble game models a computation's traffic between a small fast memory and a large slow memory, and its S-partition argument cuts the computation into pieces each with a bounded set of inputs, the same shape as an NCI block decomposition.
findings.quote: In this paper, the red-blue pebble game is proposed to model the input-output complexity of algorithms.
findings.bears_on: NCI's block decomposition is an S-partition with the memory bound S replaced by a cap of K novel bits read and a work bound of Gamma gates, so the S-partition counting argument is the natural template for NCI lower bounds.

findings.claim: With fast memory S, the FFT needs Omega(n log n / log S) I/O and classical matrix multiplication needs Omega(n^3 / sqrt(S)), and both bounds are attainable.
findings.quote: with a device of O(S) memory at least Omega(n log n/log S) (or Omega(n-cubed/square root of S), respectively) time is needed for the I/O.

quantities.condition: I/O lower bound for classical n x n matrix multiplication scales as n^3 / S^0.5; S counts all words in fast memory, with no free (committed) operands

findings.bears_on: Gives the classical per-piece work bound (work per piece at most about S^1.5 for matrix multiplication); NCI differs because committed weights are free, which removes one of the three operands from the count.

findings.claim: Hong and Kung's bounds are tight, achieved by blocked decompositions.
findings.quote: All of the lower bounds presented are the best possible in the sense that they are achievable by certain decomposition schemes.
findings.bears_on: Shows that partition-based communication lower bounds can be tight; NCI's slowdown bounds would also want matching attack constructions (decompositions) to show tightness.

title: Communication lower bounds for distributed-memory matrix multiplication
authors: Dror Irony, Sivan Toledo, Alexander Tiskin
venue: Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing 64(9)

findings.claim: 2D algorithms, with Theta(n^2/P) memory per processor, communicate O(n^2/P^(1/2)) words per processor, and this is optimal for that memory.
findings.quote: We show that the amount of communication that they perform per processor, O(n 2/P 1/2), is asymptotically optimal for this amount of memory.

quantities.condition: per-processor communication n^2 / P^0.5 with O(n^2/P) memory; conventional Theta(n^3) algorithms only

findings.bears_on: Parallel analogue of a per-block input cap: it bounds the busiest processor, as NCI bounds every block, but counts words rather than novel bits.

findings.claim: 3D algorithms replicate the inputs Theta(P^(1/3)) times and cut communication to Theta(n^2/P^(2/3)) per processor, which is optimal for that memory.
findings.quote: But this allows them to reduce the amount of communication to only Θ(n 2/P 2/3) per processor. We show that this amount of communication is optimal for the amount of memory that is used.

quantities.condition: 3D (replicated) regime, O(n^2/P^(2/3)) memory per processor

findings.bears_on: Replicating inputs buys less communication; in NCI committed theta is replicated for free, which is the regime where these bounds are weakest.

findings.claim: The bounds cover only classical cubic algorithms, not Strassen-like ones.
findings.quote: Our analysis applies only to conventional matrix-multiplication algorithms. It does not apply to Strassen’s algorithm [23] or other o(n 3) algorithms.
findings.bears_on: Any NCI bound proved by Loomis-Whitney-style counting would not cover an adversary that restructures matrix products bilinearly (Strassen-like); a different technique (expansion, Grigoriev flow, communication complexity) is needed.

findings.claim: The bounds deliberately do not charge for replicating the inputs, the analogue of NCI not charging for committed parameters.
findings.quote: our lower bounds do not even count the communication necessary to perform the replication of input elements!
findings.bears_on: Precedent for leaving initial data distribution free, as NCI does for theta; the bounds then come only from data produced during the computation.

title: No Train No Gain: Revisiting Efficient Training Algorithms For Transformer-based Language Models
authors: Jean Kaddour, Oscar Key, Piotr Nawrot, Pasquale Minervini, Matt J. Kusner

findings.claim: Layer stacking, layer dropping, selective backprop, RHO loss, Lion and Sophia lose their gains against a fully-decayed learning-rate baseline at fixed compute.
findings.quote: When pre-training BERT and T5 with a fixed computation budget using such methods, we find that their training, validation, and downstream gains vanish compared to a baseline with a fully-decayed learning rate.
findings.bears_on: Many efficient-training m_A claims fall to about 1 against a tuned baseline.

title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
authors: Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child et al.

findings.claim: LSTMs match Transformers on early-context tokens but fall behind on later tokens.
findings.quote: We see from these figures that the LSTMs perform as well as Transformers for tokens appearing early in the context, but cannot match the Transformer performance for later tokens.
findings.bears_on: The transformer's advantage is concentrated in long-context use, part of why its m_A grows with scale.

findings.claim: Kaplan's compute-optimal model size grows as C^0.73, spending extra compute mostly on parameters.
findings.quote: can be fit very well with a power-law N(C_min) ∝ (C_min)^0.73

quantities.condition: N_opt ∝ C^0.73 (Kaplan)

findings.bears_on: The allocation Chinchilla replaced; the reference recipe here is Chinchilla-optimal.

title: Scaling Laws for Fine-Grained Mixture of Experts
authors: Jakub Krajewski, Jan Ludziejewski, Kamil Adamczewski, Maciej Pióro, Michał Krutul, Szymon Antoniak et al.

findings.claim: A compute-optimal fine-grained MoE at 1e20 FLOP matches a dense Transformer with 20x the compute; the saving exceeds 40x past 1e25 FLOP.
findings.quote: Our results suggest that a compute-optimal MoE model trained with a budget of 10^20 FLOPs will achieve the same quality as a dense Transformer trained with a 20× greater computing budget, with the compute savings rising steadily, exceeding 40× when budget of 10^25 FLOPs is surpassed

quantities.condition: MoE vs dense compute-equivalent, 1e20 FLOP
MoE vs dense, beyond 1e25 FLOP

findings.bears_on: The largest growing m_A in the record; fitted on 129M-3.7B models with E = 64 experts and extrapolated.

findings.claim: The fits fix the expansion rate at E = 64 and span 129M-3.7B parameters and 16B-130B tokens.
findings.quote: To constrain the search space, E = 64 is fixed, following the recommendations of Clark et al. (2022).

quantities.condition: expansion rate E in all fits

findings.bears_on: The measured range is about 1e19-3e21 FLOP; the 40x figure is extrapolation.

title: Scaling Laws for Upcycling Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
authors: Seng Pei Liew, Takuya Kato, Sho Takase

findings.claim: An interaction between dense and upcycled dataset sizes limits upcycling's efficiency at large budgets.
findings.quote: there is a novel interaction term between the dense and upcycled training dataset that limits the efficiency of upcycling at large computational budgets
findings.bears_on: Upcycling's gain shrinks with C.

findings.claim: The fitted upcycling law: loss as a function of the dense seed's tokens D1 and the upcycled tokens D2, with an interaction term.
findings.bears_on: Gives the break-even upcycled budget D*, past which training the MoE from scratch is better.

findings.claim: Upcycling helps only while the upcycled budget stays below a threshold that shrinks with model size (4B tokens for an 8x1B model).
findings.quote: Particularly, upcycling is beneficial when D_{2} remains below a certain threshold, where the pretrained dense model can still accelerate convergence. However, beyond this threshold, from-scratch training of MoE becomes more efficient.

quantities.condition: 8x1B MoE upcycled from a 1B dense seed

findings.bears_on: A registered seed's head start is worth little to a frontier-scale new run.

title: An inequality related to the isoperimetric inequality
authors: L. H. Loomis, H. Whitney
venue: Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 55(10)

findings.claim: The volume of a set of unit cubes is bounded by the product of its coordinate projections, with equality for boxes; this is the geometric core of the matrix multiplication communication bounds.
findings.quote: Let S be a set of cubes from a cubical subdivision of n-space; let Si be the set of (n — 1)-cubes obtained by projecting the cubes of S onto the ith coordinate hyperplane.
findings.bears_on: The inequality bounds work per block only if every projection is capped; NCI leaves the weight projection (theta) and the outputs free, so it gives no useful per-block bound by itself.

findings.claim: Boxes aligned with the axes attain the bound, which is why blocked algorithms are optimal.
findings.quote: Note that for w-dimensional intervals with faces parallel to the coordinate hyperplanes, (1) holds with the equality sign.
findings.bears_on: Tightness by boxes suggests the matching NCI attack is a blocked decomposition along the token, layer and weight axes.

title: nGPT: Normalized Transformer with Representation Learning on the Hypersphere
authors: Ilya Loshchilov, Cheng-Ping Hsieh, Simeng Sun, Boris Ginsburg

findings.claim: nGPT, with every vector normalized to the hypersphere, needs 4-20x fewer training steps for equal accuracy.
findings.quote: Experiments show that nGPT learns much faster, reducing the number of training steps required to achieve the same accuracy by a factor of 4 to 20, depending on the sequence length.

quantities.condition: steps saved, lower end
steps saved, upper end, longest context

findings.bears_on: Step count, not FLOPs: nGPT's per-step cost is higher; the claimed m_A is unreplicated at scale.

title: Joint MoE Scaling Laws: Mixture of Experts Can Be Memory Efficient
authors: Jan Ludziejewski, Maciej Pióro, Jakub Krajewski, Maciej Stefaniak, Michał Krutul, Jan Małaśnicki et al.

findings.claim: Under joint memory and compute budgets, MoE models can be more memory-efficient than dense ones.
findings.quote: Surprisingly, we show that MoE models can be more memory-efficient than dense models, contradicting conventional wisdom.
findings.bears_on: MoE's gain survives a cap on total parameters, which matters if the policy bounds committed state.

title: Gemstones: A Model Suite for Multi-Faceted Scaling Laws
authors: Sean McLeish, John Kirchenbauer, David Yu Miller, Siddharth Singh, Abhinav Bhatele, Micah Goldblum et al.

findings.claim: Scaling-law prescriptions are highly sensitive to experimental design and the checkpoints used in fitting.
findings.quote: we find that the prescriptions of scaling laws can be highly sensitive to the experimental design process and the specific model checkpoints used during fitting
findings.bears_on: Multipliers read off fitted laws carry design-dependent error; small differences in m_A are not robust.

title: Do Transformer Modifications Transfer Across Implementations and Applications?
authors: Sharan Narang, Hyung Won Chung, Yi Tay, William Fedus, Thibault Fevry, Michael Matena et al.

findings.claim: In a shared codebase most proposed Transformer modifications do not meaningfully improve performance.
findings.quote: Surprisingly, we find that most modifications do not meaningfully improve performance.
findings.bears_on: Discounts single-paper m_A claims for architecture tweaks; most are near 1 once re-implemented.

title: Scaling up Masked Diffusion Models on Text
authors: Shen Nie, Fengqi Zhu, Chao Du, Tianyu Pang, Qian Liu, Guangtao Zeng et al.

findings.claim: Masked diffusion models scale at the autoregressive rate but need about 16x more compute for equal validation loss.
findings.quote: However, MDMs still require approximately 16 times more computational resources than ARMs to achieve comparable validation losses.

quantities.condition: derived 1/16: MDM vs ARM, equal validation loss

findings.bears_on: Masked diffusion m_A about 1/16, constant in C (same exponent).

title: RWKV: Reinventing RNNs for the Transformer Era
authors: Bo Peng, Eric Alcaide, Quentin Anthony, Alon Albalak, Samuel Arcadinho, Stella Biderman et al.

findings.claim: RWKV, a linear-attention RNN, performs on par with similarly sized Transformers up to 14B parameters.
findings.quote: We scale our models as large as 14 billion parameters, by far the largest dense RNN ever trained, and find RWKV performs on par with similarly sized Transformers
findings.bears_on: Linear-attention RNN m_A about 1 at matched size.

title: Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models
authors: Tomer Porian, Mitchell Wortsman, Jenia Jitsev, Ludwig Schmidt, Yair Carmon

findings.claim: The Kaplan-Chinchilla discrepancy comes from last-layer cost, warmup duration and scale-dependent optimizer tuning; corrected, Kaplan's setup reproduces Chinchilla.
findings.quote: identifying three factors causing the difference: last layer computational cost, warmup duration, and scale-dependent optimizer tuning
findings.bears_on: The Kaplan-to-Chinchilla multiplier is a methodology fix, available to anyone at no NCI cost.

title: Fast Learning Requires Good Memory: A Time-Space Lower Bound for Parity Learning
authors: Ran Raz

findings.claim: A streaming learner with less than n^2/25 bits of memory needs exponentially many samples to learn an n-bit parity.
findings.quote: We show that any algorithm for parity learning, that uses less than $\frac{n^{2}}{25}$ bits of memory, requires an exponential number of samples.

quantities.condition: derived: n = sqrt(25 K) for K = 2e7 bits (about 47,000 for K = 9e7); applies only if a single thread's K-bit block input is the learner's whole memory between blocks

findings.bears_on: If a training thread carries at most K novel bits from block to block, memory-sample tradeoffs imply exponential (not merely constant-factor) slowdowns for some learning problems with n above about 2e4-5e4.

findings.claim: With quadratic memory the same problem takes O(n) samples by Gaussian elimination, so the gap is caused by the memory bound alone.
findings.quote: Parity learning can be solved in polynomial time, by Gaussian elimination, using $O(n)$ samples and $O(n^{2})$ memory bits.
findings.bears_on: Illustrates the kind of separation a per-block cap could force on learners whose state cannot be compressed, the opposite case to low-U updates such as seed-based fine-tuning.

title: Shuffles and Circuits (On Lower Bounds for Modern Parallel Computation)
authors: Tim Roughgarden, Sergei Vassilvitskii, Joshua R. Wang

findings.claim: The MPC (s-shuffle) model caps each machine's input per round at s bits, smaller than the input, with no communication inside a round.
findings.quote: the "fan-in" of each machine is limited to s bits, where s is smaller than the input size n, and that computation proceeds in synchronized rounds, with no communication between different machines within a round.
findings.bears_on: An MPC machine-round is close to an NCI block (fan-in s ~ K), except that NCI bounds a block's work and gives committed data for free; MPC lower bounds transfer only where those differences do not matter.

findings.claim: Few-round MPC computations are low-degree real polynomials, which gives unconditional round lower bounds.
findings.quote: We prove that computations in our model that use few rounds can be represented as low-degree polynomials over the reals.
findings.bears_on: Polynomial-degree arguments could bound how far information spreads across NCI blocks per round of dependency.

findings.claim: Much stronger generic round lower bounds would separate P from NC1, so unconditional bounds for arbitrary functions are blocked.
findings.quote: Restricting to a polynomial number of machines, we show that asymptotically better lower bounds would separate P from NC 1
findings.bears_on: NCI slowdown bounds cannot come from generic circuit lower bounds; they must use the structure of training (sequential updates, b_w, b_a), as NCI's thread and sharding bounds do.

title: Observational Scaling Laws and the Predictability of Language Model Performance
authors: Yangjun Ruan, Chris J. Maddison, Tatsunori Hashimoto

findings.claim: Across about 100 public models, families differ mainly in how efficiently they convert training compute into a low-dimensional capability space.
findings.quote: we show that these variations are consistent with a simple, generalized scaling law where language model performance is a function of a low-dimensional capability space, and model families only vary in their efficiency in converting training compute to capabilities
findings.bears_on: Supports modelling a recipe as a single compute multiplier m_A on log C, the form used for C_eff.

title: The I/O Complexity of Attention, or How Optimal is Flash Attention?
authors: Barna Saha, Christopher Ye

findings.claim: FlashAttention's N^2 d^2 / M I/O is optimal for every cache size M >= d^2.
findings.quote: an I/O complexity lower bound that matches the upper bound provided by FlashAttention for any values of $M\geq d^{2}$ within any constant factors

quantities.unit: exponent of d in attention I/O
quantities.condition: I/O = Theta(N^2 d^2 / M) for M >= d^2; N = sequence length, d = head dimension

findings.bears_on: Gives a tight data-movement bound for the attention step that dominates long-session inference and training; a template for bounding attention inside an NCI block.

findings.claim: The bound survives fast matrix multiplication because it is proved through a communication complexity protocol, not by counting products.
findings.quote: even if one uses fast matrix multiplication, the above I/O complexity bounds cannot be improved. We do so by introducing a new communication complexity protocol for matrix compression, and connecting communication complexity to I/O complexity.
findings.bears_on: The most directly borrowable technique: NCI already measures information in bits, so a communication complexity lower bound for the update function would transfer to NCI regardless of how the adversary writes the circuit.

title: Rethinking LLM Advancement: Compute-Dependent and Independent Paths to Progress
authors: Jack Sanderson, Teddy Foley, Spencer Guo, Anqi Qu, Henry Josephson

findings.claim: In nanoGPT experiments, compute-independent innovations give combined CEG up to 3.5x at both scales, while compute-dependent ones hurt at small scale and approach parity as size grows.
findings.quote: Experimental validation with nanoGPT models confirms that compute-independent advancements yield significant performance gains (e.g., with combined CEG up to 3.5×) across the tested scales. In contrast, compute-dependent advancements were detrimental to performance at smaller experimental scales, but showed improved CEG (on par with the baseline) as model size increased

quantities.condition: combined CEG of compute-independent innovations, nanoGPT

findings.bears_on: Separates constant from scale-dependent m_A; under a compute cap the constant ones remain usable.

findings.claim: Multi-query and sparse attention have CEG well below 1 in a compact model and near 1 in the full model.

quantities.condition: MQA CEG, compact nanoGPT
MQA CEG, full nanoGPT
sparse attention CEG, compact
sparse attention CEG, full

findings.bears_on: Inference-oriented attention changes have m_A at or below 1 for training, rising toward 1 with scale.

title: GLU Variants Improve Transformer
authors: Noam Shazeer

findings.claim: GEGLU and SwiGLU feed-forward variants give the best perplexities among the GLU variants tested in T5.
findings.quote: The GEGLU and SwiGLU variants produce the best perplexities.
findings.bears_on: Gated FFNs are a small constant m_A with no NCI change.

title: Scaling Laws for Linear Complexity Language Models
authors: Xuyang Shen, Dong Li, Ruitao Leng, Zhen Qin, Weigao Sun, Yiran Zhong

findings.claim: Linear-complexity models (70M-7B, 300B tokens) scale like LLaMA and beat it on perplexity and commonsense reasoning at equal FLOPs, but are weaker at retrieval.
findings.quote: Our findings reveal that linear complexity models exhibit similar scaling trends to conventional transformer-based models and consistently outperform LLaMA in cross-domain perplexity and average accuracy in commonsense reasoning under the same FLOPs budget but demonstrate weakness in retrieval tasks.
findings.bears_on: m_A about 1 or slightly above on loss, below 1 on retrieval; same exponent as softmax attention.

title: Primer: Searching for Efficient Transformers for Language Modeling
authors: David R. So, Wojciech Mańke, Hanxiao Liu, Zihang Dai, Noam Shazeer, Quoc V. Le

findings.claim: Primer's gains over the Transformer increase with compute and follow a power law.
findings.quote: Experiments show Primer's gains over Transformer increase as compute scale grows and follow a power law with respect to quality at optimal model sizes.
findings.bears_on: A rare architecture tweak whose m_A grows with C.

findings.claim: At 1.9B parameters Primer uses one third of the compute for the same one-shot performance; against the original T5 at 500M it cuts training cost 4x.
findings.quote: For instance, in a 1.9B parameter configuration similar to GPT-3 XL, Primer uses 1/3 of the training compute to achieve the same one-shot performance as Transformer.

quantities.condition: Primer vs Transformer, 1.9B, one-shot
Primer vs original T5, 500M, C4 LM

findings.bears_on: m_A about 3 against a 2021 baseline; against a modern (SwiGLU, RoPE) baseline the gain is smaller.

title: Beyond neural scaling laws: beating power law scaling via data pruning
authors: Ben Sorscher, Robert Geirhos, Shashank Shekhar, Surya Ganguli, Ari S. Morcos

findings.claim: With a good pruning metric, error can in theory fall exponentially rather than as a power law in pruned dataset size.
findings.quote: show how in theory we can break beyond power law scaling and potentially even reduce it to exponential scaling instead if we have access to a high-quality data pruning metric
findings.bears_on: The one mechanism proposed for an exponent change from data selection.

findings.claim: Most existing pruning metrics scale poorly to ImageNet.
findings.quote: We find most existing high performing metrics scale poorly to ImageNet
findings.bears_on: The exponent change has not been shown for LM pretraining.

title: Scaling Laws vs Model Architectures: How does Inductive Bias Influence Scaling?
authors: Yi Tay, Mostafa Dehghani, Samira Abnar, Hyung Won Chung, William Fedus, Jinfeng Rao et al.

findings.claim: Of ten architectures, the vanilla Transformer scales best even where it is not best in absolute terms.
findings.quote: It turns out that amongst all ten architectures that we consider, the vanilla Transformer has the best scaling behaviour, even if its absolute performance at each compute region is not the greatest.
findings.bears_on: Small-scale wins of alternative architectures often reverse with scale (m_A shrinks with C).

findings.claim: Linear-attention Performer fails to scale: perplexity drops 2.7% base-to-large vs 8.4% for the Transformer.
findings.quote: Another interesting trend is that “linear" Transformers such as Performer fail to scale as shown in Figure 2(i). The pre-training perplexity metric only decreases by 2.7% going from base to large scale compared to 8.4% of the vanilla Transformer.

quantities.condition: Performer perplexity drop base->large
vanilla Transformer perplexity drop

findings.bears_on: Kernel linear attention has a worse exponent: m_A falls with C.

findings.claim: Parameter sharing (Universal Transformer, ALBERT) warps scaling in performance, FLOPs and parameters.
findings.quote: a distinct feature of Universal Transformers (and ALBERT) is parameter sharing. Hence, compared with standard Transformers, this architectural choice significantly warps the scaling behaviour not only with respect to performance but also amongst compute metrics such as FLOPs, speed and number of parameters
findings.bears_on: Shared-parameter (looped) models have few updated parameters per FLOP, which lowers updated state.

title: Transcending Scaling Laws with 0.1% Extra Compute
authors: Yi Tay, Jason Wei, Hyung Won Chung, Vinh Q. Tran, David R. So, Siamak Shakeri et al.

findings.claim: Continuing PaLM 540B with UL2's mixture of denoisers for 0.1% extra compute gives about 2x compute savings.
findings.quote: Impressively, at 540B scale, we show an approximately 2x computational savings rate where U-PaLM achieves the same performance as the final PaLM 540B model at around half its computational budget

quantities.condition: U-PaLM 540B vs PaLM 540B, downstream

findings.bears_on: m_A about 2 at about 2.5e24 FLOP on downstream metrics.

title: Towards Greater Leverage: Scaling Laws for Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
authors: Changxin Tian, Kunlong Chen, Jia Liu, Ziqi Liu, Zhiqiang Zhang, Jun Zhou

findings.claim: On 1T identical tokens, a 0.85B-active MoE matched a 6.1B dense model with over 7x less compute.
findings.quote: When trained on an identical 1T high-quality token dataset, Ling-mini-beta matched the performance of the 6.1B dense model while consuming over 7x fewer computational resources

quantities.condition: Ling-mini-beta (0.85B active) vs 6.1B dense, 1T tokens

findings.bears_on: MoE m_A above 7 at about 5e21 FLOP.

findings.claim: Efficiency leverage grows with the compute budget at a fixed activation ratio.
findings.quote: Second, for a fixed activation ratio, the EL grows with the computational budget, demonstrating that the MoE advantage is amplified at larger scales.
findings.bears_on: MoE m_A grows with C (300+ models up to 28B).

title: An Empirical Study of Mamba-based Language Models
authors: Roger Waleffe, Wonmin Byeon, Duncan Riach, Brandon Norick, Vijay Korthikanti, Tri Dao et al.

findings.claim: At 8B parameters and 1.1T tokens, pure Mamba and Mamba-2 are about 15 points behind a Transformer on 5-shot MMLU.
findings.quote: For the former, after training for 1.1T tokens, both Mamba and Mamba-2 models produce nearly 15 points lower accuracy when compared to a Transformer model on this task.
findings.bears_on: Pure SSMs lose in-context and copying ability at scale: m_A below 1 on those tasks.

findings.claim: An 8B hybrid of 43% Mamba-2, 7% attention and 50% MLP layers beats the 8B Transformer on all 12 standard tasks, by 2.65 points on average.
findings.quote: In contrast, we find that the 8B Mamba-2-Hybrid exceeds the 8B Transformer on all 12 standard tasks we evaluated (+2.65 points on average) and is predicted to be up to 8x faster when generating tokens at inference time.

quantities.condition: Mamba-2-Hybrid vs Transformer, 8B, 3.5T tokens, 12-task average

findings.bears_on: Hybrid m_A above 1 at 8B/3.5T tokens; no equal-loss compute ratio is reported.

title: Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule
authors: Songlin Yang, Jan Kautz, Ali Hatamizadeh

findings.claim: Gated DeltaNet surpasses Mamba2 and DeltaNet on language modeling, reasoning and retrieval; hybrids with sliding-window attention add training efficiency.
findings.quote: Our proposed architecture, Gated DeltaNet, consistently surpasses existing models like Mamba2 and DeltaNet across multiple benchmarks
findings.bears_on: Delta-rule recurrences improve on SSMs; m_A vs Transformer not reported.

title: Differential Transformer
authors: Tianzhu Ye, Li Dong, Yuqing Xia, Yutao Sun, Yi Zhu, Gao Huang et al.

findings.claim: Differential attention needs about 65% of the parameters or tokens of a Transformer for equal loss.
findings.quote: The scaling curves indicate that Diff Transformer requires only about 65% of model size or training tokens needed by Transformer to achieve comparable language modeling performance.

quantities.condition: derived 1/0.65: parameter or token efficiency vs Transformer, 830M-13B

findings.bears_on: m_A about 1.5 (1/0.65) on parameters or tokens separately, from 830M to 13B.

findings.claim: Fitted curves put a 6.8B Diff Transformer level with an 11B Transformer (62.2% of parameters).
findings.quote: According to the fitted curves, 6.8B-size Diff Transformer achieves a validation loss comparable to 11B-size Transformer, requiring only 62.2% of parameters.
findings.bears_on: Constant parameter-efficiency gain across the tested sizes.

title: Information-theoretic lower bounds for distributed statistical estimation with communication constraints
authors: Yuchen Zhang, John C. Duchi, Michael I. Jordan, Martin J. Wainwright

findings.claim: Reaching the centralized minimax rate for d-dimensional estimation from m machines needs about dm/log m bits of communication, even with full interaction.
findings.quote: at least $B\gtrsim\frac{dm}{\log m}$ bits are required for any distributed procedure—even allowing fully interactive communication—to attain the centralized minimax rate.

quantities.unit: bits per coordinate per machine, up to a 1/log m factor
quantities.condition: derived: total dm/log m bits over m machines and d coordinates; Gaussian mean estimation; read as a floor on how far per-shard update messages can be compressed

findings.bears_on: If a training run must split its data over m blocks (each limited to Gamma work), the aggregating blocks must read about dm/log m novel bits, a floor on b_w-like compression of per-shard updates for at least some estimation problems.

findings.claim: Communicating the answer is exponentially cheaper than computing it distributedly: O(d log(mn)) bits describe the solution, yet nearly dm bits must be exchanged.
findings.quote: there is an exponential gap between the number of bits required to communicate the problem solution and the number required to compute it in a distributed manner.
findings.bears_on: NCI's sharding cost uses U, the update's description length; this result says the novel bits needed to compute an update across blocks can far exceed U, so a sharding bound in terms of U may be loose in the adversary's favor.

findings.claim: Each machine individually must send at least d/log m bits.
findings.quote: each machine individually must communicate at least $\frac{d}{\log m}$ bits for a decentralized procedure to match the centralized rate.
findings.bears_on: A per-shard floor, comparable to NCI's per-block cap K: when d/log m exceeds K, a shard's contribution cannot fit in one block's input.

title: Accelerating Training of Transformer-Based Language Models with Progressive Layer Dropping
authors: Minjia Zhang, Yuxiong He

findings.claim: Progressive layer dropping pre-trains BERT 2.5x faster to similar downstream accuracy.
findings.quote: Extensive experiments on BERT show that the proposed method achieves a 24% time reduction on average per sample and allows the pre-training to be 2.5 times faster than the baseline to get a similar accuracy on downstream tasks.

quantities.condition: PLD vs BERT baseline, downstream accuracy

findings.bears_on: Claimed m_A 2.5 for BERT; Kaddour 2023 finds layer-dropping gains vanish.
